note: Records for the Build Power section. verification: confirmed = official page or IRS data read on the date shown; indexed = dated 2026 search results or secondary source; unverified = could not confirm 2026 activity or key facts.
intro: Voting decided who holds office. What those officials do with it depends on what happens next: who shows up at their offices, who organizes the workplaces and buildings they govern, and who runs next time.
This directory lists the groups and tools for each of those jobs.
how_to_read: Each entry says what the group does, how you can take part, its legal form, and where it sits politically. Only gifts to 501(c)(3) charities are tax-deductible; gifts to 501(c)(4)s, 527s, PACs and trade associations are not. “Confirmed” means an official page or IRS record was read on November 9, 2026. “Not confirmed” means we could not establish current activity or a key fact, and the entry says which.

records.name: The Montana Plan (Initiative 194)
records.what: A voter-passed state law that bars corporations, unions, trade associations, nonprofits and anonymous-donor groups from spending in Montana elections by redefining what powers the state grants them.

records.legal_status: Led by the Transparent Election Initiative, founded by former Commissioner of Political Practices Jeff Mangan
records.partisanship: Cross-partisan coalition; the Montana Republican Party formally opposed it
records.status_2026: Passed 65% to 34% (97% counted, Nov. 5). The same day, the Montana Republican State Central Committee and allied groups sued in federal court to overturn it.
records.notes: Vote share is unofficial until certification. Source is Montana Free Press reporting distributed via AP.

start_here.title: This week
start_here.text: Look up your officials and find a local group that meets in person: an Indivisible group or a RepresentUs Local Action Team. Set one Congress.gov alert on a bill tied to a winner’s campaign promise.

start_here.title: This month
start_here.text: Take a free training: Freedom Trainers’ Noncooperation 101 (Nov. 18, 7 pm ET) or the LGBTQ+ Victory Institute’s free Candidate & Campaign 101 (Washington DC, Dec. 3). Read three Beautiful Trouble entries: Action star, Choose your target wisely, Do your research.

start_here.title: Build economic power
start_here.text: Renters: start with the Tenants Together guide. Workers without a union: contact EWOC.

start_here.title: Run, or recruit someone
start_here.text: Find an office on RunForOffice.org or Ballotpedia’s state filing pages, then apply to a pipeline that fits (see “Run for office” in the directory below).

start_here.title: Give with intent
start_here.text: Want the deduction? Choose a 501(c)(3) such as Democracy at Work Institute, the Participatory Budgeting Project or a group’s education fund. Want lobbying muscle? Give to the 501(c)(4) arm.

data_centers.title: Data centers and your power bill
data_centers.lede: This was a top-versus-bottom fight in 2026, and it is being won locally.

points.text: On Nov. 3, voters favored limits on data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures.
In Congress, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340) 417–3 on Sept. 16; it only asks state regulators to consider making 100 MW+ data centers pay the full cost of grid upgrades.
In the Senate, Sen. Martin Heinrich blocked fast-track passage as too weak, and a Sept. 30 motion to proceed failed 57–43, short of the 60 needed.
The binding decisions sit with your state utility commission and local zoning board: file comments in large-load tariff cases and ask new governors and legislators for a mandatory standard.

data_centers.note: A separate Senate resolution, S.Con.Res. 30, only praises the White House’s voluntary pledge.

beautiful_trouble.intro: (501(c)(3); 15,000+ people trained) is a free, Creative Commons toolbox in eight languages. It has five kinds of entry:
beautiful_trouble.recommended_lede: For turning a win into lasting power, start with these entries:

recommended.name: Choose your target wisely
recommended.note: aim at whoever can sign the check or introduce the bill

recommended.name: Don’t fall in love with your tactics

beautiful_trouble.fits: “If you’re not uncomfortable, your coalition is too small” fits a top-versus-bottom coalition.
beautiful_trouble.extras: Extras: trainings, a $40 strategy card deck, and a Resistance Hotline for one-on-one action planning (current hours not confirmed). It also publishes a Palestine-solidarity tool set, which some readers will see as a political position.

solutions.name: Beautiful Solutions
solutions.text: (OR Books, 2024; edited by Elandria Williams, Rachel Plattus, Eli Feghali and Nathan Schneider) is the companion on building alternatives: co-ops, the commons, energy democracy, participatory budgeting. Each section pairs Solutions, Stories, Principles and open Questions. Beautiful Rising, gathered from Global South movements, was folded into the main toolbox in 2020.

pbp.name: Participatory Budgeting Project
pbp.text: (501(c)(3)) has free guides — a Scoping Toolkit for officials, an Outreach Toolkit, a Guide to PB in Schools — for letting residents decide part of a public budget. The usual first step is one official who controls a slice of budget and will pilot it.

open_items.title: Results still moving
open_items.body: The Montana Plan’s 65–34 margin is unofficial and the measure is in federal court. Irvine’s ranked-choice Measure D leads 52.6% to 47.4% in the latest county count reported by NBC Los Angeles; FairVote has declared it passed, but it is not certified. The Alaska and Mississippi Senate races and the Alaska and Kansas governor races were not called as of this check; Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is set for Nov. 18 and Mississippi must certify by Nov. 13.
